title: Traffic Signal Controller
summary: A timed phase state machine for one intersection with a hard safety invariant — no two conflicting directions ever green — plus emergency-vehicle preemption.

slides.markdown:
Designing a traffic light controller for one intersection looks simple — a few lights, a timer —
until the interviewer asks the one question this case study exists for: how do you guarantee two
conflicting directions are never both green, even under a bug, an interrupt, or a rushed code
change? Get `Intersection`, `SignalGroup`, `Phase`, and `Controller` sketched fast, then spend your
time proving the safety invariant is enforced structurally, not just "usually true."

Scope stays to one intersection — no network-wide coordination — which is itself worth saying out
loud.

slides.sectionTitle: Requirements: phases, timing, pedestrian crossing, emergency override
slides.markdown:
Scope it as: the intersection cycles through **phases** (which directions get green, in what
combination), each phase has a **duration**, a **pedestrian crossing** signal is tied to specific
phases, and an **emergency-vehicle override** can force a phase change out of the normal cycle.

Non-goal: coordinating with adjacent intersections for city-wide green-wave timing — that's a
distributed, multi-intersection problem worth naming as a natural follow-up, not something to
design here. One intersection's own safety and timing logic is plenty for one round.

slides.sectionTitle: Core entities: Intersection, SignalGroup, Light, Phase, Controller, Timer
slides.markdown:
`Light` is the single red/yellow/green bulb-set for one direction; a `SignalGroup` bundles the
lights that always change together — all northbound lanes, say. A `Phase` names which
`SignalGroup`s are green, and for how long, at once. `Intersection` holds all the `SignalGroup`s;
`Controller` owns the current `Phase` and a `Timer` driving transitions.

The reason `Phase` is its own entity rather than a raw duration on `SignalGroup`: a phase is a
*combination* — "NS green, EW red" — and the safety invariant is a property of combinations, not
of any single light.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: class diagram for signal groups and the shared controller
slides.markdown:
![Intersection, SignalGroup, Controller, and Phase relationships](assets/traffic-signal-class-diagram.svg)

One `Controller` per `Intersection` is deliberate: it's the single authority deciding which
`Phase` is active, so there's exactly one place the safety invariant has to be enforced, not one
per `SignalGroup`.

assets.alt: Intersection, SignalGroup, Controller, and Phase relationships

slides.markdown:
![Phase cycle with all-red clearance between every transition](assets/traffic-phase-cycle.svg)

`all-red clearance` sits between every pair of conflicting-direction phases, never skipped. It
exists specifically so a car still clearing the intersection under a yellow light isn't met with
cross-traffic already moving — cutting straight from one green combination to the next is the
classic real-world collision cause this state machine avoids by construction.

assets.alt: Phase cycle with all-red clearance between every transition

slides.sectionTitle: Code: Controller.tick() advancing phases on a timer
The hard part: 'no two conflicting directions are ever green'
slides.markdown:
The invariant sounds obvious stated in English, and is exactly the kind of thing a rushed edit —
adding a new phase, tweaking a duration — can silently violate if it isn't enforced in code. A
developer adding a new left-turn phase six months from now shouldn't be trusted to manually
re-verify every combination by eye.

The fix is structural, not procedural: represent every phase's SignalGroup-to-light-color mapping,
and check any proposed transition against a **conflict matrix** before it's ever applied. The
invariant becomes something the code enforces, not something a human has to remember.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a conflict-matrix check before switching any Light
Compare: hardcoded phase sequence vs data-driven phase table
slides.markdown:
| | Hardcoded sequence | Data-driven phase table |
|---|---|---|
| Adding a new phase (e.g. protected left turn) | edit Controller's transition logic directly | add a row to a config/table read at startup |
| Changing timing for one intersection type | requires a code change and redeploy | a different table file per intersection |
| Risk surface | every change touches the class enforcing safety | only ConflictMatrix and Controller's core loop need review for safety |

**How to decide:** intersections vary a lot — four-way, T-junction, protected turns — and their
phase tables change more often than the controller logic itself should. Data-driven wins once you
support more than a couple of intersection shapes.

An emergency vehicle approaching should be able to force an early transition to a phase that
clears its path, without abandoning the safety invariant — the forced phase still has to pass
`ConflictMatrix.isSafe()`, and the return to the normal cycle has to resume cleanly rather than
getting stuck.

I'd model preemption as an interrupt request `Controller` checks at the top of every `tick()`,
ahead of the normal timer check: a pending request resolves into an early `transitionTo()` call —
through the same safety check as any other transition — and the controller remembers where the
normal cycle left off so it can resume once the preemption clears. Keeping the interrupt as a
single well-defined "requested action to apply" avoids a special-cased branch scattered through
the timer logic.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: modeling all-red clearance as an afterthought
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "The main phases are NS-green and EW-green; I'll just insert a brief pause
between them if there's time."

**Why it's wrong:** treating the clearance interval as an optional pause rather than a first-class
`Phase` means it's easy to skip under time pressure — a preemption interrupt or a buggy
phase-table edit can jump straight from one green combination to the conflicting one, precisely
the collision the whole design exists to prevent.

**Correct model:** `all-red clearance` is a `Phase` like any other, subject to the same
`ConflictMatrix` check and the same phase-table entry — not a gap between phases, but one of them.
